passages.where: A single proverb sets two states side by side: hope deferred makes the heart sick, and desire fulfilled is a tree of life. The site's note calls it one of the Bible's most honest lines about longing. Scripture does not tell the person who has waited years that the ache is imaginary or faithless; it names the sickness of the heart before anything else.

Jacob works seven years for Rachel, and they seem but a few days because of his love for her. The site's note calls it the tenderest line about love between a man and a woman in Genesis, and observes that Laban's words sounded like consent without quite promising what Jacob asked. The Bible honors the longing, and the next verses show that getting what you long for does not end every sorrow.

Naomi, widowed in a foreign land, blesses her two widowed daughters-in-law with the hope that the LORD will let each of them find rest in the home of a new husband. The site's note tells how famine and death had stripped the family to three women. The wish for a home and a companion is spoken as a blessing in Scripture, and asked of God, not hidden as a weakness.

David says his soul waits quietly for God alone, and then calls everyone to trust him at all times and pour out their hearts before him. The site's note says he holds that status and wealth are only a breath, while power and loving devotion belong to God. Longing is meant to be poured out to God in full, not tidied up first.

The psalm praises God as father of the fatherless and defender of widows, the God who settles the lonely in families. The site's note says the psalm celebrates him as father of the fatherless and defender of widows. A spouse is one way God answers loneliness, and the family of his people is another, open to everyone.

Paul, himself single, says each person has a particular gift from God, one of one kind and one of another, and then tells the unmarried and widows that it is good to stay as he is, and good to marry. The site's plain note speaks to single readers who did not choose it or have not chosen it yet: the passage does not ask you to explain yourself, you are not unfinished, and a church that treats single people as a problem to be solved has not listened to Paul or to Jesus.

Anna, a prophetess widowed after seven years of marriage, has lived alone for decades and worships in the temple night and day. The site's note says her description reads like a portrait of faithful Israel waiting, and that she is the first in Luke to speak of Jesus to others in the temple. The plain note adds that a life many would call empty, old, widowed and alone, can be full before God.

From prison Paul says he has learned to be content in any situation, filled or hungry, with plenty or in need. The site's plain note says the strength Christ gave him was the strength to be content, a prisoner's peace rather than a promise that circumstances will change. Contentment, on Paul's account, is learned over time, and it does not require pretending that a desire is gone.

In the middle of the Bible's bleakest book, the speaker says the LORD is good to those who wait for him, and that it is good to wait quietly for his salvation. The site's note says the hope in this chapter is chosen rather than felt. Waiting here is not passive resignation but a deliberate turning toward God while the answer has not come.

The chapter that began with comfort for exiles ends with the promise that those who wait upon the LORD will renew their strength, mount up like eagles, run and not grow weary. The site's note says the unwearied God gives his strength to the weary. The promise is strength for the waiting, not a date when the waiting will end.

misread.taken: Delight yourself in the LORD and he will give you the desires of your heart is often given to single people as a promise that if they are devoted enough, God will send them a husband or wife, and the long wait can then feel like proof that their devotion has fallen short.
misread.says: The site's plain note answers that the verse does not mean God will give whatever you want if you are religious enough. The first half comes first: when God himself is your delight, your desires change. The promise is not a method for getting things but a picture of a heart that wants God most and finds that he does not disappoint. The psalm is counsel against fretting while waiting, and nowhere does it measure anyone's faith by whether they have married.

whole: The longing for marriage is good and God-given, and its ache, unmet, can go very deep. It shows up at weddings and baby showers, at church events built for couples, in the quiet of a Sunday afternoon, in the questions of relatives who mean well, and in the slow arithmetic of age. Some carry it alongside the grief of a broken engagement or a marriage that ended, or with the knowledge that the years for children may be closing. Some have tried everything they were told to try and wonder what is wrong with them. Many Christians add a heavier question: whether the waiting means God is withholding, or that they have not been faithful enough to be given what they ask.

Scripture does not shame the desire. It calls hope deferred a sickness of the heart, it records Jacob's seven years that seemed a few days, and it puts Naomi's prayer for her daughters' rest in a husband's home on the lips of a faithful woman. It is also honest about why the waiting is so heavy. Marriage has become, in many churches and families, the measure of a finished adult life, and single people are treated as a problem to be solved, which the site's notes say plainly is not how Paul or Jesus spoke. Our own hearts add to the weight when a spouse becomes the thing we believe will finally make us whole, a weight no human being can carry. Many of us who are married have treated single friends as if they were waiting to begin their lives, and that too is part of the burden.

So the Bible's wisdom is to hold the longing honestly before God without letting it become the measure of your life. Pour out your heart to him, as the psalm says, and keep asking; Naomi did. Take reasonable, ordinary steps without treating them as a test of faith, and let trusted friends speak into them. Refuse the lie that the wait is a verdict on your worth or your devotion; Psalm 37 promises that delight in God changes desire, not that devotion earns a spouse. Learn contentment the way Paul did, over time and in real circumstances, which is not the same as pretending the desire is gone. Invest in the friendships, service and family of God that are yours now. And if you are part of a church, ask whether single people there are treated as whole members or as people in a waiting room.

The hope Scripture gives is that God has not overlooked you, and that your life is not on hold. Paul and Jesus lived full lives unmarried, and Anna, alone for decades, was among the first to recognize the Christ. God settles the lonely in families, sometimes by a marriage and always through his people. Those who wait for the LORD will renew their strength, even when the waiting is long. And every human marriage, the Bible says, points beyond itself to the union of Christ and his people, a wedding to which every believer, married or single, is invited. The longing you feel is not foolish. It is meant, in the end, to be met.
sit: What have you been told your waiting means about your faith or your worth, and what does God himself say about it?

prayer.lead: A prayer to the God who opens his hand to every living thing. Pray it with the desire you carry, and leave it in his hand.

But Anna shows that a life many would call empty, old, widowed and alone, can be full before God.
